meta.tagline: Behind the yachts and beach clubs, a fishing village is still hiding — finding it takes a little time

pills: Eat Tarte Tropézienne at Place des Lices
Get lost in La Ponche neighbourhood

overview.intro: When you hear Saint-Tropez, you think yachts, beach clubs and Brigitte Bardot. All true — but in summer this face of the city is so dominant that the real Saint-Tropez becomes hard to see. Until the 1950s this was a small fishing village nobody knew about. The traces of that village are still here today: colourfully painted fishing boats in the old harbour, elderly men playing pétanque under the plane trees of Place des Lices, the stone streets of La Ponche neighbourhood. To reach them, skip the peak season or set out very early in the morning. Saint-Tropez is small — everything is within walking distance. But getting here is another story: no train station, and traffic seizes up completely in summer.

local_word.definition: The French boules game — metal balls thrown to land closest to the target ball, a game that can be played for hours. Under the plane trees of Place des Lices, elderly Tropéziens play in the mornings and late afternoons. Watching is free; to join you need to wait for an invitation. One of Saint-Tropez's most authentic and accessible local experiences — just a few steps from the yacht harbour.

rules.title: If you must come in July-August, book well in advance
rules.description: In midsummer the roads around Saint-Tropez are gridlocked for hours, beaches overflow and prices peak. If you have to come during this period, book at least three months ahead. If coming by car, leave it in the out-of-town car parks and take the shuttle bus into the centre. Very early morning and after 7pm the town gets a little breathing room.

rules.title: Plan your transport — there's no train station
rules.description: No train goes to Saint-Tropez. The nearest train station is Saint-Raphaël, then a bus ride of 1-1.5 hours. Ferry from Sainte-Maxime is 25 minutes — much more enjoyable. Summer season ferry from Nice is about 2.5 hours. If you hire a car, traffic in midsummer is very bad; people who don't plan their transport in advance lose a lot of time.

rules.title: Not the harbour front — go to La Ponche and the Citadelle side
rules.description: The cafés and restaurants on the harbour front are Saint-Tropez's most expensive and most touristy spots. La Ponche neighbourhood, the Citadelle slope and the area around Place aux Herbes are both cheaper and far more local. Go to Place des Lices for Tarte Tropézienne; for food, explore the streets behind the harbour.

quick_facts.sub: Ferry from Sainte-Maxime 25 min · bus from Saint-Raphaël 1–1.5 hrs

quick_facts.sub: Beach clubs are paid · free sections also available · by bike or car

quick_facts.label: Weather
quick_facts.sub: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct ideal · Jul–Aug crowded and expensive · Dec–Feb quiet

quick_facts.label: Food
quick_facts.sub: Harbour front expensive · La Ponche and side streets reasonable

tip.label: Place des Lices market — Tuesday and Thursday mornings
tip.text: A morning market set up in the shade of plane trees on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Local cheeses, olives, Provençal spices, fresh fruit and vegetables, handmade goods. Open 8am-1pm. The original Tarte Tropézienne shop is also on this square. You can watch the pétanque players and sit on the square with a coffee. Saint-Tropez's most local and most free experience.

overview.title: Welcome to Saint-Tropez

transport.intro: Getting to Saint-Tropez isn't easy — no trains, roads are narrow and jammed in summer. The ferry is the most enjoyable option.

items.title: Ferry — the best option
items.description: Les Bateaux Verts ferry from Sainte-Maxime reaches Saint-Tropez in 25 minutes. Daily sailings April-October. Return approximately €16-18. Trans Côte d'Azur ferry from Nice runs direct during summer season (June-September) — about 2.5 hours, enjoyable but long. Ferry connections also available from Saint-Raphaël. Book tickets in advance in summer.

items.title: Bus — cheap but slow
items.description: Varlib/ZOU! route 7601 from Saint-Raphaël train station goes to Saint-Tropez. About 1-1.5 hours, €2-3. Can stretch to 2-3 hours in summer traffic. Bus connections also available from Les Arcs-Draguignan train station. Budget-friendly but requires patience.

items.title: Car — freedom but traffic
items.description: Your own car or a hire car is the most flexible option — essential for seeing the surrounding villages. But the N98 road is gridlocked for hours in midsummer. Solution: leave the car at Les Marines de Cogolin or Port Grimaud car parks 3-4km from town and get to the centre by shuttle bus or boat. Parking in town is both expensive and nearly impossible.

items.title: Bicycle — ideal for Pampelonne
items.description: Saint-Tropez centre is small and walkable but Pampelonne beach is 5 kilometres away — a bicycle is the smartest choice. Many hire points in and around town. The cycling path to Pampelonne is partly shaded. Electric bikes are also available — more comfortable for the hilly sections.

items.title: Walking — sufficient within town
items.description: Saint-Tropez centre is genuinely small: from the harbour square to Place des Lices is 5 minutes, La Ponche 7 minutes, the Citadelle 15 minutes. The entire historic centre is walkable. The Sentier du Littoral coastal walking trail extends all the way to Pampelonne — about 35km, requires a full day.

callout.label: Port Grimaud — the French version of Venice with gondolas
callout.text: 8 kilometres north-west of Saint-Tropez, a canal city built in the 1960s. Houses open directly onto the water; small boat tours are available. Ideal for stopping before or after the Sainte-Maxime ferry. There's a free outer area to walk; boat tours of the inner canals are ticketed. A calmer alternative away from Saint-Tropez's crowds.

transport.title: Getting Around

stay.intro: Saint-Tropez and surroundings — the town itself is expensive; surrounding villages are both more affordable and more authentic.

local_word.definition: The old fishing neighbourhood hidden behind the harbour square, at the foot of the Citadelle. Narrow stone streets, colourfully painted windows, old fishermen's houses. Touristy but still quiet and authentic. In the early morning hours there's almost no one here. As close to the real Saint-Tropez as you can get — just a few steps from the bustle of the harbour square.

items.name: Saint-Tropez centre
items.description: The harbour square, Place des Lices and La Ponche all within walking distance. Prices very high in summer — finding a room under €200 is difficult. The right place if you want to be close to the yacht harbour. Early booking essential.

items.name: Ramatuelle — hilltop village
items.description: 10km south of Saint-Tropez, a medieval village among vineyards and olive groves. 10 minutes to Pampelonne beach by bike or car. Half the price of Saint-Tropez, much quieter. Small restaurants, local market and a Provençal atmosphere in the village itself. Car essential.

items.name: Gassin — panoramic hilltop village
items.description: A medieval village looking down over the bay. On France's 'most beautiful villages' list. 7km from Saint-Tropez, reached by car. Small but impressive — narrow streets, bay views, a few restaurants.

items.name: Sainte-Maxime
items.description: On the opposite shore of the bay, 25 minutes from Saint-Tropez by ferry. Prices noticeably lower. Has its own beaches, restaurants and shopping street. Take the morning ferry to Saint-Tropez and return in the evening. Ideal base if you're making many day trips.

items.name: Port Grimaud
items.description: A canal city built in the 1960s — every house has a boat mooring out front. 10 minutes from Saint-Tropez by car or boat connection. Walkable within itself, restaurants along the canals. A good option for escaping the crowds.

stay.title: Where to Stay

best_time.intro: Saint-Tropez is a completely different place depending on the season — crowded and expensive in midsummer, beautifully different in spring and autumn.

items.label: Spring
items.name: The best time
items.description: April and early May are Saint-Tropez's golden period. Temperatures 18-22°C, no crowds, prices half those of midsummer. Vineyards lush, the bay clear. It starts filling up from early June but still far from the July-August crowds. No restaurant reservations needed, space on the beaches.

callout.label: Bravade festival — mid-May
callout.text: Every year from 16-18 May, a festival held in honour of Saint-Tropez's patron saint, Saint Torpès. Traditional costumes, musket fire, street processions and celebrations. Entirely local — not touristy. Being in town during this period means seeing how Saint-Tropez preserves its own identity.

items.subtitle: Spring · Fewer crowds, reasonable prices, vineyards lush

items.label: Summer
items.name: Crowded and expensive
items.description: July and August are Saint-Tropez's most intense period. Pampelonne beach is packed, roads gridlocked, hotel prices are staggering. That said, the beach clubs are at their liveliest and evenings are long and glamorous. Very early morning and after 7pm the town gets a little breathing room. June is more manageable; July-August is genuinely very crowded.

callout.label: Pampelonne — beach club or free section
callout.text: Along the 5km stretch of beach there are both paid clubs (Nikki Beach, Club 55 and others) and free public sections. Sunbed and umbrella at clubs €30-80. The free sections have the same sea — just a little more walking. Pampelonne by bike: hire from central points, 15-20 minutes.

items.subtitle: Summer · Beach season, yachts, prices at their peak

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Second best time
items.description: September and October see the crowds go, the weather stays warm and the sea remains swimmable. Grape harvest around Ramatuelle and Gassin — vineyards turn golden. No restaurant reservations needed, prices have dropped. From November some venues close but the town itself keeps going.

callout.label: Grape harvest tour — September-October
callout.text: Some wine producers around Ramatuelle and Gassin open to visitors during the harvest period. Côtes de Provence rosé comes from this area. Small family estates offer tastings and tours. 15-20 minutes by car from Saint-Tropez. Research in advance and book — estates are small, capacity limited.

items.subtitle: Autumn · Grape harvest, sea still warm, peaceful atmosphere

items.label: Winter
items.name: Quiet and local
items.description: From December to February Saint-Tropez belongs almost entirely to its residents. Many restaurants and boutiques are closed but what remains is genuinely local. Pétanque is played at Place des Lices, morning coffee at Café Sénéquier. Temperatures 10-15°C, some rainy days but many sunny moments too. Prices are a fraction of midsummer.

callout.label: Saint-Tropez in winter — the real face
callout.text: If you want to stay in Saint-Tropez in winter, look for open hotels and guesthouses in advance — options are limited. Those that are open charge around 20-30% of summer prices. The harbour is quiet, boats are moored, streets are silent. The morning market still runs. During this period it's possible to talk to Tropéziens and feel the spirit of the fishing village.

items.subtitle: Winter · Empty streets, real Tropéziens

best_time.title: When to Go

monthly_highlights.text: Les Bravades: the village's 500-year-old patron saint procession — musket volleys, costumes and true Tropezian pride.
Jet-set peak: superyachts in the port, clubs on the beach; book everything far ahead and love the morning and evening hours.
Les Voiles de Saint-Tropez: the classic sailing regatta — the gulf fills with white sails and the village turns its most elegant.
The sweet season: everything open, the crowds not yet arrived; after the mimosa, before the crush — the village at its best.

eat.intro: Eating in Saint-Tropez is expensive — but find the right place and it's both delicious and reasonable. Avoid the harbour front, step into the side streets.

local_word.definition: Invented in 1955 by a Polish pastry chef named Alexandre Micka. A double-layered brioche pastry with orange blossom aroma — filled with a vanilla and creamy filling. Brigitte Bardot loved this pastry, and it was she who gave it the name 'Tarte de Saint-Tropez'. The original recipe is still a secret. La Tarte Tropézienne shop at Place des Lices — in the same spot since 1955.

items.name: Tarte Tropézienne
items.description: Buy it from the original La Tarte Tropézienne shop at Place des Lices. Whole tart €25-35, a slice €5-8. Fresh in the morning. The orange blossom aroma is subtle, the filling creamy. Eating this pastry here is one of Saint-Tropez's most local and most accessible rituals.
items.tag: Place des Lices, La Tarte Tropézienne · slice €5–8

items.name: Fresh fish — at Place aux Herbes
items.description: The small fish market at Place aux Herbes runs in the mornings — the Tropézien fishermen's daily catch is sold here. If you want fresher and cheaper fish than the tourist restaurants on the harbour front, go to the small bistros around Place aux Herbes. Get there early before it sells out.
items.tag: Around Place aux Herbes · early morning · fresh daily catch

items.name: Ratatouille
items.description: Courgette, aubergine, tomatoes, peppers, onions and garlic — Provence's most pure vegetable dish. Every local restaurant in Saint-Tropez makes it; both as a main dish and alongside meat and fish. In summer, the version made with vegetables from the local market is the finest. Can also be eaten cold in the summer heat.

items.name: Daube Provençale
items.description: Provence's beef stew slow-cooked in red wine. Prepared with olive oil, onions, garlic, thyme and bay leaf, simmered slowly for hours. A winter and spring dish — rarely seen on summer menus. Between September and May, findable at small restaurants around La Ponche.

items.name: Côtes de Provence rosé
items.description: From the vineyards surrounding Saint-Tropez, France's most famous rosé. Pale in colour, light in aroma, dry in character — Provence rosé is exported around the world. But the best is drunk here. A glass at cafés on Place des Lices or the bars near the harbour: €6-10.
items.tag: Every café and bistro · glass €6–10 · away from the harbour

items.name: Socca and pissaladière — at Place des Lices market
items.description: At the Tuesday and Thursday morning market, local stalls sell chickpea flour pancake (socca) and onion tart slices (pissaladière). €2-4, the best morning snack. Try both as you browse the market stalls — the cheapest and most delicious way to have a Provençal breakfast.
items.tag: Place des Lices market · Tues and Thurs · €2–4

callout.label: Café Sénéquier — harbour icon
callout.text: Historic café with a red awning on the harbour square — in the same spot since 1887. Expensive (espresso €5-7) but worth sitting at least once. The best spot for watching the mega yachts and harbour life. If you go for breakfast between 8am and 10am, it's much less crowded than at midday or in the evening.

eat.title: What to Eat

hidden_gems.intro: Saint-Tropez's finest corners are usually a few minutes from the harbour square or in the surrounding villages.

items.name: La Ponche — the old fishing quarter
items.description: Just behind the harbour square, a few steps in. Narrow stone streets, colourfully painted windows, old fishermen's houses. Bardot filmed And God Created Woman here in 1956 and introduced Saint-Tropez to the world. It still carries the spirit of that film. In the early morning hours there's almost no one here. Small restaurants and cafés exist but most open in the afternoon.
items.rarity: Brigitte Bardot's Saint-Tropez — La Ponche neighbourhood

items.name: Gassin — medieval village overlooking the bay
items.description: 7km from Saint-Tropez, 15 minutes by car. On France's 'Les Plus Beaux Villages' list. The village with the best panoramic view of the bay — nothing obstructing it, just sea. Small church, narrow streets, a few restaurants. Coming here for dinner means escaping the crowds below and gaining the view.
items.rarity: From France's most beautiful villages list — Gassin

items.name: Citadelle de Saint-Tropez
items.description: A 17th-century castle on the hill east of town. Contains a maritime history museum inside. But the real reason: the panoramic view of Saint-Tropez bay from the moat and ramparts around the castle. Ticketed but reasonably priced. Quietest in the early morning hours. Standing here looking out at the harbour, Pampelonne and the distant Estérel mountains, you understand why the town became so beloved.
items.rarity: The Citadelle and the town's finest view — affordable

items.name: Sentier du Littoral — coastal path
items.description: A coastal walking trail from Saint-Tropez extending to Pampelonne and Ramatuelle. 35km in total but can be done in sections. Rocky shores, small coves, pine forests and Mediterranean views. Hot in July-August; spring and autumn are ideal. Walking it, you find your own secret cove — an experience far beyond Saint-Tropez's beach club facade.
items.rarity: Sentier du Littoral — coastal walking trail

items.name: Musée de l'Annonciade
items.description: Five minutes from the harbour square, in a former chapel. Signac, Matisse, Derain, Bonnard — Post-Impressionist and Fauvist painters lived and worked in Saint-Tropez at the start of the 20th century. This museum holds their works. If it's very hot outside or the harbour is too crowded, stepping into this museum means both cooling down and seeing genuinely fine art. Little-known but of real quality.
items.rarity: Not a museum — a real Provençal experience

items.name: Port Grimaud
items.description: 8km from Saint-Tropez, a canal city built from scratch in the 1960s by architect François Spoerry. Venice-like but Provençal — every house has a boat mooring out front, colourfully painted facades. Boat tours are ticketed; the outer area is free to explore. Perfect for stopping before or after the Sainte-Maxime ferry.
items.rarity: Port Grimaud — Provençal village on canals

callout.label: Place des Lices — pétanque and shade
callout.text: The town's central square but not touristy — mornings and late afternoons, elderly Tropéziens play pétanque here. Plane tree shade, dusty ground, the sound of metal balls. Watching is free and never gets old. Tuesday and Thursday market is set up on this square. The original Tarte Tropézienne shop is here too. Saint-Tropez's least touristy and most local corner.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Gems

items.label: Eat Tarte Tropézienne — at Place des Lices
items.sub: Original La Tarte Tropézienne shop. Slice €5-8. Orange blossom flavour, creamy filling. Fresh in the morning.

items.label: Walk La Ponche neighbourhood in the early morning
items.sub: Behind the harbour square. Narrow stone streets. Almost no one in the early morning hours. Bardot's Saint-Tropez.

items.label: Watch pétanque at Place des Lices
items.sub: Mornings and late afternoons. Elderly Tropéziens playing. Under the plane trees. Free.

items.label: Go to the Tuesday or Thursday morning market
items.sub: Place des Lices. 8am-1pm. Local cheese, olives, socca, pissaladière. Best between 8am and 10am.

items.label: Come by ferry from Sainte-Maxime
items.sub: Les Bateaux Verts. 25 minutes. Return ~€18. Take the early morning sailing and arrive at an empty harbour.

items.label: Have a morning coffee at Café Sénéquier
items.sub: Same spot since 1887. Expensive but worth it once. Between 8am and 10am is quietest.

items.label: Climb the Citadelle — for the bay view
items.sub: 17th-century castle. Ticketed but affordable. Panoramic view. Quietest in the early morning.

items.label: Go to Gassin village
items.sub: 7km from Saint-Tropez. 15 minutes by car. On France's most beautiful villages list. Breathtaking bay view.

items.label: Cycle to Pampelonne beach
items.sub: Hire bikes in the centre. 15-20 minutes. Free sections available too. Beach clubs €30-80 for sunbeds.

items.label: Visit Musée de l'Annonciade
items.sub: 5 minutes from the harbour square. Matisse, Signac, Derain. Not crowded. Cool refuge on hot days.

items.label: Walk part of the Sentier du Littoral
items.sub: Coastal path, extends to Pampelonne. Can be done in sections. Find your own secret cove.

items.label: Drink Côtes de Provence rosé
items.sub: Every bistro and café. Glass €6-10. Cheaper away from the harbour. It comes from these very lands.

checklist.title: Saint-Tropez Checklist
checklist.completion_message: Saint-Tropez will draw you back for a quieter season — by fishing boat, not by yacht.

traps.title: Skip the Traps
traps.intro: Saint-Tropez's fame shows up in its prices, but the village itself is still a small fishing town. Know these four and live it without the jet-set bill.

items.name: A club sunbed at Pampelonne
items.description: At the famous beach clubs, a sunbed plus lunch easily reaches hundreds of euros; the sea is the same sea for everyone.
items.instead: Lay your towel on Pampelonne's public stretches or pick the path-access coves; if the clubs intrigue you, go for just a drink.

items.name: Dining at yacht-view prices on the port front
items.description: The quay cafés add the superyacht view to the menu: an ordinary salad, an extraordinary bill.
items.instead: Watch the yachts for free walking the quay; eat two streets in, on the La Ponche side.

items.name: Driving in through summer traffic
items.description: In July and August the single access road is an hours-long queue; parking is a separate war.
items.instead: Park in Sainte-Maxime and cross the gulf in 15 minutes by sea shuttle (bateau vert): the view is a bonus, the calm is free.

items.name: Buying a 'celebrity hunt' tour
items.description: The boat tours pointing at star villas from afar are an expensive disappointment; celebrities are on the port anyway when they want to be seen.
items.instead: Spend the same money on the coastal path (Sentier du Littoral): coves, headlands and the real Saint-Tropez view.

callout.label: The golden rule
callout.text: In Saint-Tropez the clock is the rule: the village belongs to locals before 9 am and after 7 pm. Give the hours between to the beach, the hill villages and the path.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: Port, La Ponche and a Gassin sunset

steps.title: Port and La Ponche morning
steps.description: Fishing boats on the quay, then the pastel lanes of the old quarter; before the crowds, the village is yours.

steps.title: Climb to the Citadelle
steps.description: From the 16th-century fort the gulf lies at your feet; the maritime museum inside tells the village's real story.

steps.title: Place des Lices
steps.description: If it's Tuesday or Saturday, the market feast; if not, watch pétanque under the plane trees and buy the tarte Tropézienne at its source.

steps.title: Lunch — Place aux Herbes
steps.description: The little square's fish stall and bistros: the day's catch, a glass of rosé.

steps.title: Pampelonne or the coastal path
steps.description: Either the sea on the public beach, or cove-to-cove walking on the Sentier du Littoral.

steps.title: Sunset in Gassin
steps.description: From the hill village's terrace the gulf turns crimson; dinner on the village square, with daube.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Live the village as a guest, not a tourist

steps.title: The village classics
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: port, Citadelle, Lices, Gassin.

steps.title: Coastal path day
steps.description: Walk the Sentier du Littoral in the morning (from Plage des Graniers to the coves), a long sea break in the afternoon, fish at La Ponche at night.

steps.title: Hill villages and vineyards
steps.description: Ramatuelle's lanes in the morning, a vineyard tasting at noon (a domaine like Minuty), the canals of Port Grimaud in the afternoon, farewell with a tarte Tropézienne.

phrases.title: The 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Provençal French is slow and sunlit; these five are enough in the village.

items.meaning: Hello — the mandatory first word of every exchange
Please — add it to the end of your order
Cheers! — rosé glasses rise to this
The Provençal exclamation: 'oh my / poor thing' — hear it and you've arrived in the south
